newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. agency sees hope in Taleban anti-drug stance.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency sees hope in Taleban anti-drug stance.

text.p: A United Nations official said on Thursday he hoped a new anti-narcotics stand taken by the powerful Taleban movement will help curb the thriving drug trade in war-ravaged Afghanistan.

Giovanni Quaglia, director of the U.N. International Drug Control Programme (UNDCP) in Islamabad, told Reuters that the rise of the radical Islamic militia, which now controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, had made little difference to widespread opium cultivation and trafficking so far.
But he said the Taleban had declared in writing this month that they opposed the production, consumption and marketing of drugs and wanted to enforce U.N. drug control resolutions.

"The UNDCP will work constantly with Taleban in this particular aspect to make sure that what they have written will be complied with, and we have strong reason to believe that the Taleban will comply with the promise," he said.
Quaglia said the Taleban declaration was issued two weeks after he had held talks at the movement's headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar on November 3.
The Taleban statement, issued by the Foreign Ministry, described narcotics abuse as a "repugnant and evil deed".

"Struggle against narcotics and their abuse...forms the focal point of the Islamic government of Afghanistan and...it will take the necessary measures for the implementation of the UNDCP conventions," the statement said.
Quaglia said opium production in Afghanistan had stabilised at around 2,400 tonnes in the last two years with about 200,000 families involved in opium poppy cultivation.
Taleban leaders have previously said they cannot ban poppy cultivation immediately because farmers in the impoverished countryside needed alternative ways to earn a living.

The biggest opium-producing provinces in Afghanistan, including Helmand and Nangarhar, are under the control of the Taleban. The movement seized the capital Kabul on September 27, but its government has yet to gain international recognition.
The Taleban have vowed to impose their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law throughout Afghanistan.
